newsitem.title: VATICAN: Pope urges Netanyahu, Arafat to break deadlock.
newsitem.headline: Pope urges Netanyahu, Arafat to break deadlock.

text.p: Pope John Paul has urged Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Palestinian President Yasser Arafat to restart the stalled Mideast peace process, telling them he is very worried by a deadlock in dialogue.
The Vatican on Thursday released the texts of two letters the Pope sent to the leaders on June 16 urging them to redouble their efforts.

In his letter to Netanyahu, the Pope called for "courageous compromises" that would earn him the gratitude of all humanity and in his missive to Arafat, the Pontiff said the painful history of the past must not prove "vain and useless".
"The Pope wanted to stimulate the leaders to make a serious effort to get the process going again," chief Vatican spokesman Joaquin Navarro-Valls told reporters.

In the letters, the Pontiff said that a Holy Land at peace would be a worthy way of welcoming the many pilgrims expected to visit the region for the start of the third millennium of Christianity in the year 2000.

"It must be admitted that the much hoped-for dialogue between the parties, and in particular between the government over which you preside and the leaders of the Palestinian people, is practically at a standstill," he told Netanyahu.
The latest deadlock in the talks began in March after Israel started work on a Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem.

The Palestinians see the work as an Israeli bid to preempt final status peace talks on the fate of the city, which Palestinians want to be the capital of a future state. Israel regards East Jerusalem as part of its capital.
Earlier this week, Egyptian Foreign Minister Amr Moussa said that Arab-Israeli peace negotiations had reached their lowest point in 20 years.

The Pope did not mention the settlement dispute but told Netanyahu that the heavy burden of suffering on both sides "deserves the utmost commitment to finding the paths of necessary and courageous compromises."

The Pope told Netanyahu that he was writing out of "my profound sense of suffering, which I believe certainly corresponds to the sadness and perhaps even the frustration of the majority of Israelis and Palestinians."

In his letter to Arafat, the Pope spoke of a "de facto interruption of dialogue" and added: "My fear is that if this situation continues it will become increasingly difficult to revive the quest for the trust that is essential to every negotiation."
The 77-year-old Pope has met both men and has accepted their invitation to make his first visit to the Holy Land.
The Pope has said he would like to make the historic visit before the year 2000.
He did not mention his desire in the letters but said millions of Jewish, Christian and Moslem believers from around the world would want to visit in the next few years.
"Also and especially for this reason there should be peace, so that the meaning of the approaching Great Jubilee of the year 2000 may be complete," the Pope told Arafat.
Egyptian envoy Osama el-Baz is to resume a mediation bid between Israel and the Palestinian Authority next week.
Egypt stepped up its mediation efforts after the United States failed to defuse a crisis over the East Jerusalem settlement.

Israel says it has the right to build on lands it captured in the 1967 Middle East war and Netanyahu says Arafat must crack down on militants and restore security cooperation with the Jewish state before talks can resume.
